content: Naphtha refers to a group of flammable liquid mixtures composed of hydrocarbons. It is typically derived as a component of natural gas condensate or as a distillation product from petroleum, coal tar, or peat. Naphtha is a volatile, aromatic liquid that ranges in color from colorless to reddish-brown and shares similarities with gasoline. In petroleum engineering, full-range naphtha is defined as the fraction of hydrocarbons in crude oil that boils between 30°C and 200°C. This fraction is composed of hydrocarbon molecules containing 5 to 12 carbon atoms and constitutes approximately 15–30% of crude oil by weight. Light naphtha, which boils between 30°C and 90°C, contains hydrocarbons with 5–6 carbon atoms, while heavy naphtha, boiling between 90°C and 200°C, contains hydrocarbons with 6–12 carbon atoms. Naphtha is primarily used as a feedstock for producing high-octane gasoline through catalytic reforming. It is also employed as a diluent in bitumen mining, as a feedstock for olefin production in petrochemical steam crackers, and as a solvent in the chemical industry. Common consumer products made with naphtha include lighter fluid, camp stove fuel, and certain cleaning solvents. The term naphtha originates from Latin and Greek, which in turn borrowed it from Persian. In Ancient Greek, it referred to petroleum or pitch. The word appears in Arabic as nafţ (نَفْط) and in Hebrew as neft (נֵפְט). Historical accounts indicate that Arabs and Persians distilled petroleum for tar and fuel in ancient times. The term naphtha is also mentioned in the Septuagint, where it describes a miraculous flammable liquid. The word is etymologically linked to naphthalene and phthalate and is part of the term napalm, which derives from naphthenic acid and palmitic acid. Historically, naphtha was used to mean crude oil, but this usage is now obsolete in English. However, in some languages, such as Ukrainian, Belarusian, and Persian, the word still refers to crude oil. In other regions, such as Italy, Serbia, and Argentina, nafta colloquially refers to diesel fuel or gasoline. Naphtha poses significant health and safety risks. Certain forms of naphtha may be carcinogenic, and products labeled as naphtha often contain impurities with harmful properties. As a product of the refining process, naphtha is a complex mixture of chemicals, making it difficult to identify specific carcinogens. Light naphtha primarily consists of straight-chained and cyclic aliphatic hydrocarbons with 5 to 9 carbon atoms, while heavy naphtha contains hydrocarbons with 7 to 9 carbon atoms. The World Health Organization (WHO) categorizes health effects into three types: reversible symptoms (Type 1), mild chronic encephalopathy (Type 2), and severe chronic toxic encephalopathy (Type 3). Benzene, a known carcinogen, is often present in naphtha mixtures, and its content is typically specified in Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS). Naphtha is highly volatile and can explode when exposed to high temperatures, as evidenced by a fatal explosion at the Avon Refinery in California in 1999. Physically, naphtha has a molecular weight of 100–215 g/mol, a density of 750–785 kg/m³, and a boiling point of 160–220°C. It is a colorless or red-brown liquid with a kerosene-like or aromatic odor and is insoluble in water. It is incompatible with strong oxidizers. In petroleum refineries, naphtha is obtained as an intermediate product during the distillation of crude oil. It is a volatile, flammable liquid with a specific gravity of approximately 0.7. Naphtha types are distinguished by their density, paraffin content, olefin content, naphthene content, and aromatic content, as determined by PONA or PIONA analysis. Paraffinic naphtha, which is less dense, has a higher paraffin content and is used as a feedstock in the petrochemical production of olefins. When heated in steam crackers, it produces olefins such as ethylene, propylene, and butadiene, which are used to manufacture plastics, synthetic fibers, and industrial chemicals. When used in catalytic reforming, paraffinic naphtha produces aromatics like benzene, toluene, and xylene, which are used in fuel blending, PET production, and solvents. Heavier naphtha types, richer in naphthenes and aromatics, are used in catalytic reformers to produce high-octane reformate. These types are also referred to as Straight Run Benzene (SRB) or Heavy Virgin Naphtha (HVN). Naphtha has various other applications, including as an unprocessed component in gasoline production, as an industrial solvent, and as a cleaning fluid. It is used in oil painting, shoe polish, lighter fluids, and as a fuel for portable stoves and lanterns. Historically, it was likely an ingredient in Greek fire. It is also used in fire performance equipment, as a coating for lithium metal, and as a cleaning solution for watch parts. In the furniture industry, naphtha is used to preview the patina of wood before finishing. Examples of naphtha-based products include Shellite, a highly flammable solvent used in camping stoves, and Ronsonol, a lighter fluid with a low flashpoint.
